title: In Two Decades, E-discovery Has Changed and Stayed the Same
author: Deana Uhl

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s work-redesign framing and extends it with a concrete e-discovery analogue: technology reallocates routine work to in-house teams and non-lawyer specialists while preserving outside expertise for complex matters. It reinforces selective deployment and operating-model adaptation, though it does not directly assess generative AI’s jagged capability or verification risks.
qs: In the past, many legal departments outsourced their preservation and collection work, but today’s technology capabilities have made it easier for in-house counsel to do that work and reserve outside counsel for second review and highly complex matters.
Many companies now rely on e-discovery practitioners—that may not be lawyers but bring legal process and technology expertise—to manage e-discovery tasks and program management.

kp.k: E-discovery expands beyond litigation amid budget and regulatory pressures
kp.d: In this August 13th, 2019 practitioner commentary, Uhl describes approximately two decades of e-discovery evolution, rather than AI-specific developments or measured research findings. She argues that its expanding remit, data-breach disputes and new regulations increase pressure on in-house teams even as they face expectations to reduce budgets.
qs: Today, e-discovery has expanded beyond litigation, now integral to regulatory activities, data privacy, records management and information governance.
Pressure on in-house legal teams is rising with the increase in disputes around data breaches and the addition of stringent new global regulations, alongside expectations to reduce budgets.

kp.k: Broader technology adoption accompanies consolidation and long-term partnerships
kp.d: Uhl reports growing adoption of multifunction platforms, project management tools and integrated processes. She links increased market consolidation to scaling corporate legal department needs and greater reliance on long-term partners supporting broader programs, without providing adoption rates or transaction data.
qs: Legal teams are increasingly adopting project management principles and tools to enable them, while at the same time rolling more processes into their toolsets.

Consolidation has been rapid in the e-discovery market for many years, but we’re seeing even more of it now, as the needs of corporate legal departments scale up and they increasingly lean on long-term partners that can support broader program development.

kp.k: Technology cannot replace consistent processes or human capabilities
kp.d: Despite technological advances and consolidated toolsets, Uhl argues that teams still struggle to use advanced features appropriately. Her recommendation prioritizes people, then process, then technology as the basis for preparedness and long-term cost containment.
qs: Even with the consolidation of toolsets and the advancements in technology, there is still no silver bullet to solve every e-discovery challenge.
As always, the implementation of consistent, repeatable processes is essential.
People, process and technology—in that order of priority—are critical to achieve e-discovery preparedness and cost containment over the long-term.

kp.k: Proactive playbooks replace reactive e-discovery responses
kp.d: Uhl asserts that most companies now understand their litigation profiles and develop playbooks for recurring scenarios. As anecdotal support, she describes her former in-house team's standard-process overview, which she credits with improving consistency, efficiency and cost effectiveness; no quantified outcomes are supplied.
qs: Reactive responses are expensive, stressful and laden with risk.
Most companies today know their litigation profile and proactively develop playbooks for their most common e-discovery scenarios.
We created an overview of our standard processes, which led to a more consistent, efficient and cost-effective approach to each e-discovery exercise.

kp.k: Proportionality and reasonableness increasingly shape e-discovery rulings
kp.d: Uhl reports greater emphasis on proportionality and more consistent preservation and spoliation rulings, referencing Rule 37e's spirit of reasonableness without identifying individual cases. She maintains that understanding one's data environment remains important for negotiating scope and making proportionality arguments.
qs: Proportionality has become a significant factor in e-discovery court orders, and cases are continually pushing forward on improved proportionality standards.
Similarly, preservation and spoliation rulings are becoming more consistent, with the courts emphasizing the Rule 37e spirit towards reasonableness in preservation and spoliation sanctions.

With regard to proportionality, legal teams that deeply understand their own data environments continue to be in a much better position for negotiating e-discovery scope and arguing for what’s proportional.

kp.k: Cooperation remains difficult despite judicial expectations
kp.d: Uhl distinguishes courts' expectation of reasonable, good-faith agreement from practitioners' continuing difficulty cooperating. She acknowledges progress on search terms and scope but reports persistent obstacles during meet and confer conferences.
qs: Generally speaking, the courts expect parties to reach reasonable agreement on e-discovery in good faith, and this is widely agreed to be the ideal.
While progress has been made on better cooperation around search terms and scope, we’re still seeing many lawyers struggle to reach easy agreement in meet and confer conferences.

kp.k: Privacy regulation complicates preservation and production obligations
kp.d: Uhl identifies GDPR, the California Consumer Privacy Act and other data-protection laws as expanding e-discovery responsibilities. Although she says cross-border case volume has not changed dramatically, she predicts that regulatory maturation will require more teams to balance disclosure and privacy. She recommends mapping data flows and assessing preservation and collection capabilities against competing duties to protect or destroy data.
qs: While the volume of cross-border cases has not changed dramatically, as GDPR and data protection regulations in other jurisdictions mature, more legal teams will be tasked with balancing the review and production of personal information with privacy requirements.

Specifically, teams must look at their data footprint to determine where data flows in and out of the organization, what technology and process capabilities are needed to preserve and collect that information for e-discovery purposes and how legal obligations to preserve and produce certain data intersect with privacy obligations to destroy and protect it.

kp.k: Blended personal and corporate data does not excuse noncompliance
kp.d: Uhl asserts that courts continue to expect preservation and collection of relevant data despite the difficulties created by intermingled personal and corporate information. This is presented as a continuing judicial expectation, not a finding tied to specified decisions.
qs: Courts are not sympathetic to companies that do not preserve and collect data that comes into scope for e-discovery.
Personal and corporate data is blended within most organizations, and courts maintain the expectation that counsel will find a way to deal with the related challenges.

kp.k: Technology enables insourcing and redistributes work to outside counsel
kp.d: Uhl describes in-house teams taking greater responsibility for legal holds, collection and first-level review. She attributes the shift from outsourced preservation and collection to improved technology capabilities, with outside counsel reserved for second review and highly complex matters.
qs: In-house teams are owning a bigger piece of the pie on the left side of the EDRM, taking control over processes such as legal hold, collection and first-level review.

In the past, many legal departments outsourced their preservation and collection work, but today’s technology capabilities have made it easier for in-house counsel to do that work and reserve outside counsel for second review and highly complex matters.

kp.k: Nonlawyer practitioners gain responsibilities while external expertise remains important
kp.d: Uhl reports companies relying on practitioners who combine legal-process and technology expertise, whether or not they are lawyers, to manage tasks and programs. She simultaneously argues that legal, regulatory and technological knowledge remains essential and that lawyers' continuing discomfort with technology sustains reliance on outside partners.
qs: Many companies now rely on e-discovery practitioners—that may not be lawyers but bring legal process and technology expertise—to manage e-discovery tasks and program management.
In-depth knowledge of case law, changing regulations and emerging technology is still critical for e-discovery professionals to be effective.
Also, many lawyers remain uncomfortable with technology and how to use the tools. Thus, reliance on outside partners that bring expertise in these areas has stayed steady.

kp.k: Continuing technological change requires adaptable legal teams
kp.d: Uhl predicts further evolution in e-discovery technology and recommends flexibility, technology adoption and responsiveness to unexpected demands. This is a forward-looking practitioner recommendation, not a quantified forecast.
qs: The types of technology available to support and streamline e-discovery will also continue to evolve.
Legal teams must be flexible and agile to embrace change, adopt new technology and rise to unexpected demands as they emerge.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Deana Uhl makes no explicit AI-specific claims. Her claims concern e-discovery technology generally: greater adoption and consolidation, more work brought in-house, and expanded roles for non-lawyer practitioners, subject to continuing dependence on people, processes and specialist support.
pts.d: Uhl reports that legal teams are adopting platforms and project-management tools across more functions, while corporate demand for broader programs and long-term partners is contributing to market consolidation. She attributes the ability to bring preservation and collection work in-house to contemporary technology capabilities, with outside counsel reserved for second review and highly complex matters. She also observes that companies increasingly use practitioners with legal-process and technology expertise who need not be lawyers. These are not claims about AI automation or lawyer replacement. Her central qualification is that technology alone cannot solve e-discovery challenges; consistent processes and human expertise remain essential.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is Uhl’s qualitative professional observations and an example from her previous in-house role, not quantified research or AI performance evidence.
pts.d: Writing as an FTI Consulting managing director, Uhl presents the article as her overview of topics discussed in an Exterro webcast. She offers first-hand experience of developing standard processes for systems likely to fall within e-discovery scope, which she says improved consistency, efficiency and cost-effectiveness. That example supports her preparedness and process claims, rather than independently establishing the broader market-adoption or insourcing claims. She supplies no adoption statistics, cost measurements, benchmarks or named cases demonstrating technology-driven changes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article compares the early 2000s with August 2019 and predicts continued technological evolution without a specific forecast horizon.
pts.d: Uhl’s adoption, consolidation and insourcing statements describe developments observed by the article’s publication on August 13, 2019, against roughly two decades of e-discovery practice. Her forward-looking claim is that supporting technology will continue to evolve and legal teams will need to adapt. She explicitly conditions effective, cost-contained e-discovery on people and repeatable processes, not technology alone. Continuing lawyer discomfort with technology also qualifies any suggestion that insourcing eliminates the need for outside expertise.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments, outside counsel, non-lawyer e-discovery practitioners and specialist external partners.
pts.d: Corporate legal departments take greater control of legal hold, collection and first-level review while facing budget and regulatory pressures. Outside counsel’s described role shifts toward second review and highly complex matters. Non-lawyer practitioners gain responsibility for tasks and program management through their combination of process and technology expertise. External specialist partners remain important where lawyers lack technological comfort, even as more work moves in-house. The article does not quantify employment effects or predict the elimination of any of these roles.
